chunks: "I can't connect a BLDC to the microcontroller directly because the pins can only supply milliamps and the motor needs amps at maybe 12 or 24 volts.
So I need a power stage in between. The chain is: microcontroller, gate driver, three half-bridges made of six N-channel MOSFETs, then the motor.
The MCU's job is to generate PWM signals.
A good motor-control MCU has an advanced timer with three complementary PWM channel pairs and programmable dead-time, so the high and low switch in each leg never overlap.
Those six logic signals go into a three-phase gate driver, which level-shifts and supplies the amps of gate current needed to switch the MOSFETs quickly.
The high sides are usually driven with bootstrap capacitors. Then the feedback: three Hall sensor outputs go to GPIO or timer capture inputs, so I know the rotor sector.
If it's sensorless, I put the phase voltages through dividers into comparators or ADC channels.
I want a current shunt on the low side or the DC link, with an amplifier into an ADC for the current loop and overcurrent protection, plus a divider for bus voltage.
I also want a hardware fault path, an over-current comparator wired to the timer's break input so the PWM shuts off in nanoseconds without waiting for software.
Supporting parts are a DC bus capacitor, a regulator for the 3. 3 volts logic and the 10 to 12 volts gate supply, and decoupling.
Or if I want something quick, I use an integrated three-phase driver IC, so the MCU only provides PWM and Hall inputs."
